overview:
In Jain thought, the paired terms "Āgama" and "Siddhānta" name both a body of scriptures and a theory of scriptural authority. Etymologically, āgama means "that which has come down"—teaching transmitted from an authoritative source through a lineage of hearers and reciters—while siddhānta means "established conclusion" or "validated doctrine." Together, they mark the distinction between the wider stream of remembered teachings and the subset of those teachings that a community recognizes as doctrinally decisive. Rather than a single, universally fixed "Jain Bible," Jain traditions organize their scriptural world through these overlapping notions of transmission and correctness.

Historically, the early Jain canon grew out of the discourses (śruta-jñāna) of the Tīrthaṅkaras, especially Pārśvanātha and Mahāvīra, delivered in the samavasaraṇa preaching hall and remembered by chief disciples (gaṇadharas) and later monks known as śruta-kevalins. These teachings were first preserved orally in Prakrit, especially Ardhamāgadhī, and only centuries later written down and systematized. Councils at Pāṭaliputra and Vallabhi in the first millennium CE attempted to stabilize the corpus, producing the Śvetāmbara list of canonical Āgamas: Aṅgas, Upāṅgas, Cheda-sūtras, Mūla-sūtras, Prakīrṇakas, and Cūlikā-sūtras. Within this framework, "Āgama" refers to the canonical texts themselves, while "Siddhānta" can denote the doctrinal content distilled from them and from related scholastic works.

Sectarian history, especially the great schism between Śvetāmbara and Digambara communities after the famine in Magadha, profoundly shaped how Āgama and Siddhānta are understood. Śvetāmbara traditions affirm that substantial portions of Mahāvīra’s teachings survived in their Prakrit canon, even though one major text—the twelfth Aṅga, Dṛṣṭivāda—is acknowledged as lost. Digambara traditions, by contrast, hold that the original Āgamas were ultimately lost after the time of Bhadrabāhu and therefore do not accept the Śvetāmbara canon as authentic. For Digambaras, doctrinal authority (siddhānta) resides instead in later but still ancient works such as the treatises of Kundakunda and the Tattvārtha-sūtra, as well as in a broader scholastic literature. Thus, while both major sects speak of Āgama and Siddhānta, they map these terms onto different textual corpora.

Despite these differences, the conceptual role of Āgama and Siddhānta is similar across Jain traditions. Āgamas are revered as vehicles of the Jina’s insight into reality: they describe the structure of the cosmos, the nature of souls (jīvas) and karmic matter, the path of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, and the disciplines of monastic and lay life. Siddhānta, in turn, is the doctrinal backbone extracted from these texts and their commentaries: the settled teachings on categories such as the seven tattvas (fundamental realities), the three jewels (ratnatraya), vows (vratas), and stages of spiritual development (guṇasthānas). In practice, Siddhānta is not only a set of propositions but also a lived interpretive tradition, maintained through monastic study, commentarial writing, and community education.

The language and form of Āgama and Siddhānta literature reflect this dual function. Early canonical works are typically composed in terse sūtra style, using mnemonic phrasing in Prakrit to aid oral transmission. Later doctrinal treatises and commentaries, often in Sanskrit, elaborate these sūtras into systematic philosophy, ethics, and cosmology. For example, the Ācārāṅga-sūtra focuses on ascetic conduct and non-violence, while the Sūtrakṛtāṅga explores doctrinal debates; the Tattvārtha-sūtra presents a concise, aphoristic summary of Jain ontology and soteriology that both Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions accept as authoritative. Works like Kundakunda’s Samayasāra and Pañcāstikāya further refine the Siddhānta by emphasizing the pure standpoint of the soul and the classification of substances.

In contemporary Jain communities, "Āgama" and "Siddhānta" also function as educational and devotional categories. Canonical texts are recited, studied in paṭhaśālās, and used in ritual contexts, while Siddhānta is taught through catechisms, doctrinal manuals, and sermons that translate technical concepts into guidance for lay practice. Modern scholarship and community education often distinguish between primary canonical sources (tier A), traditional commentaries (tier B), and later explanatory works (tiers C and D), but within Jain religious life these layers are woven together: the authority of Siddhānta depends on its perceived continuity with Āgama, and the living understanding of Āgama is shaped by Siddhānta. The result is a dynamic scriptural tradition that preserves ancient teachings while continually rearticulating them for new contexts.

Because Jainism lacks a single universally agreed list of scriptures, it is important to see Āgama and Siddhānta not as rigid labels but as relational terms. They mark how communities negotiate continuity with the Jina’s teaching, how they decide which texts and interpretations are binding, and how they balance respect for inherited canons with recognition of historical loss and sectarian divergence. This plural yet principled approach to scripture is one of the distinctive features of Jain religious thought.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga-sūtra (Acaranga-sutta)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the gaṇadharas; redacted by Devardhigaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa in the Śvetāmbara tradition
primary_sources.original_text: णं च खलु एतं भणियमाणं अहिंसा महाव्रतं, ण हन्तव्वं ण बाधव्वं, ण विणासव्वं सव्वे पाणे
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇaṃ ca khalu etaṃ bhaṇiyamāṇaṃ ahiṃsā mahāvrataṃ, ṇa hantavvaṃ ṇa bādhavvaṃ, ṇa viṇāsavvaṃ savve pāṇe
primary_sources.translation: And thus it is declared: non-violence is the great vow; no living beings are to be killed, harmed, or destroyed.
primary_sources.notes: The Ācārāṅga-sūtra is one of the principal Śvetāmbara Āgamas and belongs to the Aṅga class. Composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, it sets out the fundamental rules of ascetic conduct, emphasizing carefulness (apramatta) and non-violence (ahiṃsā) toward all living beings. As a canonical Āgama, it is a key source for monastic discipline and is frequently cited in discussions of Jain ethics and the practical side of Siddhānta.

primary_sources.title: Sūtrakṛtāṅga (Sutrakratanga-sutta)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jain teachers; preserved in the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text: एवं मे सुतं: सव्वे पाणा बहुविहा, बहुविहं तेसं आयं, बहुविहं तेसं गयणं, बहुविहं तेसं दुखं
primary_sources.transliteration: evaṃ me sutaṃ: savve pāṇā bahuvihā, bahuvihaṃ tesaṃ āyaṃ, bahuvihaṃ tesaṃ gayaṇaṃ, bahuvihaṃ tesaṃ dukhaṃ
primary_sources.translation: Thus have I heard: all living beings are of many kinds; manifold are their births, manifold their goings, manifold their sufferings.
primary_sources.notes: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga is another major Aṅga of the Śvetāmbara Āgama collection. It addresses doctrinal issues, including classifications of living beings, karmic processes, and critiques of non-Jain views. As part of the Āgama corpus, it contributes to the canonical basis for Jain cosmology and ethics, and its teachings are integrated into later Siddhānta through commentaries and doctrinal summaries.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra (Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (accepted by both Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions)
primary_sources.translation:
Liberation is the realization of the true nature of reality.
The mutual support of living beings is their nature.
primary_sources.notes: The Tattvārtha-sūtra is a foundational doctrinal treatise, often classified as Siddhānta rather than Āgama in the narrow sense, yet it functions as a pan-sectarian scripture. Written in Sanskrit, it systematically presents Jain ontology, cosmology, ethics, and the path to liberation in aphoristic form. Both Śvetāmbara and Digambara communities regard it as authoritative, and extensive commentarial traditions elaborate its brief sūtras into detailed Siddhānta. The famous phrase "parasparopagraho jīvānām" is widely cited as a concise expression of Jain ethical interdependence.

primary_sources.title: Samayasāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text:
समयसारोऽयमुक्तोऽत्र जीवस्य स्वस्वरूपकथनात्।
नान्यदस्ति परं तत्त्वं स्वात्मदर्शनमेव हि॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
samayasāro'yamukto'tra jīvasya svasvarūpakathanāt.
nānyadasti paraṃ tattvaṃ svātmadarśanameva hi.
primary_sources.translation:
This is called the essence of the self, for it speaks of the true nature of the soul.
There is no higher reality than the vision of one’s own self.
primary_sources.notes: Samayasāra, composed in Prakrit with later Sanskrit recensions, is a central Digambara Siddhānta text. Kundakunda emphasizes the pure standpoint (niścaya-naya) of the soul, distinguishing it from karmic modifications and worldly identifications. While not part of the Śvetāmbara Āgama canon, it is treated as authoritative doctrine in the Digambara tradition and illustrates how Siddhānta can be grounded in texts outside the early canonical lists, especially where those lists are considered lost.

primary_sources.title: Pañcāstikāya
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda (Digambara tradition)
primary_sources.original_text:
जीवाज्जीवोऽस्तिकायो, अज्जीवोऽस्तिकायो च।
धम्मोऽस्तिकायो, अधम्मोऽस्तिकायो, आकाशोऽस्तिकायः॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
jīvāj jīvo'stikāyo, ajjīvo'stikāyo ca.
dhammo'stikāyo, adhammo'stikāyo, ākāśo'stikāyaḥ.
primary_sources.translation:
Of the existent categories, soul is an extended substance, and non-soul is also an extended substance.
Dharma is an extended substance, adharma is an extended substance, and space is an extended substance.
primary_sources.notes: Pañcāstikāya sets out the five extended substances (astikāyas) recognized in Jain ontology: jīva, ajīva, dharma, adharma, and ākāśa. It is a key Digambara Siddhānta text that systematizes metaphysical categories derived from earlier teachings. By articulating these categories in a concise doctrinal form, it exemplifies how Siddhānta crystallizes the conceptual content of Āgama-like traditions into a structured philosophical framework.

misconceptions.myth: There is a single, universally agreed Jain "Bible" called the Āgama, accepted in identical form by all sects.
misconceptions.reality: Jain traditions share core teachings but do not share a single fixed canon. Śvetāmbara communities preserve a specific Prakrit Āgama collection, while Digambara communities hold that the original Āgamas were lost and ground their Siddhānta in other early and scholastic works. Both use the terms Āgama and Siddhānta, but they apply them to different textual corpora and emphasize different lines of transmission.

misconceptions.myth: Siddhānta is merely a later human invention and has no direct connection to the original teachings of the Jinas.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain usage, Siddhānta denotes doctrine that is understood to be continuous with the Jina’s teaching, even when expressed in later systematic treatises and commentaries. While historical processes of loss, redaction, and interpretation are acknowledged, Siddhānta is seen as the distilled, validated understanding of the path to liberation derived from Āgama and its living study, not as an arbitrary innovation disconnected from the original insight.

misconceptions.myth: Only texts explicitly labeled "Āgama" are authoritative; all other Jain works are secondary and optional.
misconceptions.reality: Canonical Āgamas hold a special place, especially in Śvetāmbara tradition, but Jain communities also treat certain non-Āgama works—such as the Tattvārtha-sūtra and Kundakunda’s treatises—as highly authoritative Siddhānta. Authority is determined by perceived continuity with the Jina’s teaching, acceptance within a lineage, and doctrinal coherence, not solely by the presence of the word "Āgama" in a title.

misconceptions.myth: Sectarian differences about Āgama and Siddhānta mean that Śvetāmbara and Digambara Jains have completely different religions.
misconceptions.reality: Although Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions differ over the preservation and status of specific texts, they share core metaphysical and ethical commitments: belief in the 24 Tīrthaṅkaras, the reality of karma, the goal of liberation, and the centrality of non-violence and self-discipline. Their disagreements about Āgama and Siddhānta concern questions of textual history and doctrinal formulation within a broadly shared spiritual framework.
